newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Tired gold market ignores U.S. study - FT analysts.
newsitem.headline: Tired gold market ignores U.S. study - FT analysts.

text.p: Gold market players are becoming hardened to bad news, according to delegates at the Financial Times Gold Conference here on Monday.
That is why the price barely moved on Monday after reports late last Friday of a U.S. study advocating that world central banks should sell their gold reserves.
Gold bullion was valued at the $341.40 at the London afternoon fix on Friday and on Monday it was $341.50.
"The fear of central bank sales is well discounted in the price," was the dry comment of one senior official of a leading bullion bank.
The report from a Fed economist and three other analysts issued by the U.S. Federal reserve said gold as a government reserve asset was not beneficial and banks should sell.
The net gain to banks would be $370 billion and the main losers would be gold miners. Central bank gold reserves total about 35,000 tonnes, or about 17 years of annual new mine production.
The report, which was not to be seen as reflecting the views of the Fed, said the impact on gold would be to reduce the price by about $41 an ounce.
"That highlights living in the academic world as opposed to living in the real world," said a delegate, suggesting the price would fall much further.
But another said: "The market is tired. We have had a series of these scares and each one produces less impact than the last".
For instance, the IMF announced last year it would sell some of its reserves to help prop up the world's poorest countries early in the next century. The price fell about $7.

Then Switzerland announced early this year it planned to revalue its gold reserves and sell some of the surplus. The news that one of gold's staunchest advocates as a reserve asset would do such a thing knocked the price down about $5.
Germany's recent public row over revaluing reserves had a $1 impact in price, the delegate said.
The pragmatics of following up the researchers' plan was roundly dismissed by gold industry executives and observers here.
"There is no co-ordination in central bank sales now, so how could they agree and co-ordinate something as massive as this," one asked.
An official of the bank of France took the opposite view to the U.S. study.

"Gold represents long-term confidence in a currency and is an asset of last resort. It remains the ultimate currency if all confidence in banks disappears," said Jean-Pierre Patat of the French central bank.
However, the future of the gold price is uncertain enough without central banks unloading reserves wholesale, delegates said.
"We saw this as a turning-point year for gold, " said one leading analyst asking not to be named. "And the new direction was southward."
Low inflation, lack of investor interest and the potential mobilisation if not actual sales of central bank gold reserves, were the main weights on the market, he said.
Another delegate pointed out that gold demand was not growing as quickly as it had been even at relatively low prices.
"If prices go up demand will be killed off at least for a period," he said. --Brian Spoors, Prague newsroom +42 02 24230003
